title: Pentagon asked the Baltic states to tone down warnings about Russia
summary: Reuters, citing three European officials and one US official, reports that Pentagon officials including policy chief Elbridge Colby asked Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia and others in recent weeks to moderate public statements about the Russian threat. One example cited was Estonian PM Kristen Michal calling Putin a rat in a corner. The Pentagon said it won't comment on private conversations; the Baltic defence ministries did not respond.
corroboration: One original report (Reuters). Dozens of outlets repeated it, which adds reach, not corroboration.
analysis: Credible outlet and several sources, but nothing on the record yet. A European official quoted by Reuters pointed out the irony: Baltic intelligence services have been among the calmer voices. It fits the US push for a negotiated end to the war that includes sanctions relief for Russia. Watch for on-the-record Baltic responses.

title: NATO's top commander in Latvia: the threat is real, but no need to dramatise
summary: General Alexus Grynkewich, NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Europe, told journalists in Latvia that Russia's war in Ukraine shows its willingness to use force, that the alliance is already prepared for existing threats, and that resilience and preparedness are what matter.
corroboration: Reported by LETA and Baltic outlets.
analysis: Calm but vigilant, in line with Baltic intelligence assessments. Notable that NATO's military leadership and the Pentagon's political message point in the same direction this week.

title: German brigade starts electronic surveillance of Kaliningrad and Belarus
summary: The head of the Bundeswehr's Cyber and Information Domain Command told Reuters on 28 October that about 170 electronic-warfare personnel are deployed in Lithuania from 23 October to 7 December, intercepting signals to give early warning of military activity in Kaliningrad and Belarus.
corroboration: Reuters, confirmed by Bundeswehr and a German state ministry.
analysis: Strengthens NATO's early-warning picture right where this briefing has the least visibility. It also means that in future, 'nothing reported' from this sector carries more weight.

title: Sabotage arrests in Germany, Poland and Romania
summary: Munich prosecutors say two Belarusian men, aged 39 and 50, have been in custody since 7 October for plotting to set fire to infrastructure near Nuremberg on behalf of a foreign power, for payment. Der Spiegel, citing security sources, says that power is Russia. Romania links the same men to the 14 September arson at a Brașov defence plant; a Ukrainian was arrested in Warsaw.
corroboration: Prosecutors, Romanian intelligence and several independent outlets.
analysis: Prosecutors did not name Russia; the attribution comes from security sources and Romania's intelligence service. The pattern, cheap recruits from third countries paid for one-off jobs, matches the Leipzig drone case that Germany formally blamed on Russian military intelligence. Moscow denies all such accusations.

title: Fourth Russian cargo ship loads armour at Baltiysk
summary: Satellite images from 23 October show the cargo ship Lady R at the Baltiysk naval base with armoured and logistics vehicles waiting to load, after three other ships loaded similar equipment on 15–16 October.
corroboration: Two OSINT groups; reported by Ukrainian and Russian independent outlets.
analysis: The loading is documented, the destination is not. These sanctioned ships have previously supplied Russia's Africa Corps via Tobruk in Libya. Equipment leaving Kaliningrad would reduce local capacity, not build it up. Videos framing this as a Kaliningrad invasion go well beyond the evidence.

title: Russia's mobilization: no decree, but call-ups never stopped
summary: Foreign Policy argues that Russia has been legally mobilized since 2022 and has run a year-round draft since January, so a new announcement may never come. CNN reports coercive recruitment of vulnerable men.
corroboration: Consistent across independent outlets.
analysis: Earlier Ukrainian predictions of a formal mobilization from October have not come true as a decree. The manpower appears to go to the Ukraine front. No sign of new units being formed toward the Baltic direction.

title: Estonia pushes back on reported Pentagon request to soften its tone
summary: After Reuters reported that Pentagon officials asked the Baltic states to tone down warnings about Russia, Estonian PM Kristen Michal told Delfi he would not hold back and called Putin a dictator who kills women and children. Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said the US made no official proposal; ministry secretary general Jonatan Vseviov said he knew of no official request. Estonia's defence ministry declined to comment on anonymous-source reporting. Lithuania and Latvia have not commented.
corroboration: Estonian statements via Delfi, ERR and LSM; Reuters remains the only source for the request itself.
analysis: The Estonian answers do not fully line up: the foreign ministry denies any official request, while the prime minister says allies are asking Estonia to hold back. Both can be true if the pressure was informal, which is what Reuters described. Lithuanian and Latvian silence is notable.

title: One network linked to Starlink arson attacks in Lithuania, Bulgaria and Poland
summary: Lithuanian police said on 29 October that two men in their early 20s, dual German citizens living in Germany, are suspected of forming a terrorist group and of the 18 October arson attempt at a Vilnius data centre storing Starlink equipment. They were detained in Germany on a Bulgarian warrant over a 9 October fire near Sofia. Police say the 23 September attack on a Starlink station in Poland is linked to them. Turkey detained 85 people on 27 October in raids on a crime gang suspected in the Polish attack.
corroboration: Lithuanian, Polish and Turkish authorities; LRT, The Insider, Turkish Minute and others.
analysis: The cross-border link is now official. The Russian link is stated by Poland's intelligence minister and Lithuania's prime minister, and press reports say the gang's alleged leader lives under Russian protection; Lithuanian police say the motive is not yet established. The targets support Ukraine's communications, which fits the pattern of cheap proxy sabotage seen elsewhere.

title: Region-wide blackout in Kaliningrad overnight
summary: Around midnight on 31 October power went out in Kaliningrad and towns including Gvardeysk, Svetlogorsk and Bagrationovsk, and mobile internet was disrupted. The governor's press secretary said emergency automation at the CHP-2 power plant shut down part of the equipment and the load was redistributed; power is being restored in stages.
corroboration: Russian regional authorities; Kyiv Independent and UNN say the cause could not be verified.
analysis: Nothing so far contradicts the technical explanation, and there is no sign of an attack or of military activity. Headlines saying the cause is unknown run ahead of the evidence in the other direction. Worth watching only if outages repeat.

title: Report: US presses Lithuania to let Belarusian potash through Klaipėda
summary: Politico, citing four European officials, reports that US special envoy to Belarus John Coale has asked Lithuanian diplomats about easing restrictions on Belarusian potash, which EU sanctions bar from EU ports. Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said the sanctions ban both imports and transit; national security adviser Deividas Matulionis warned of legal and financial consequences.
corroboration: One original report (Politico), relayed by LRT; Lithuanian responses on the record.
analysis: Lithuania's refusal is on the record; the US request itself is not. Together with the Pentagon story, it suggests Washington is leaning on Baltic positions as it seeks a deal involving Minsk and Moscow. The State Department did not respond.

title: Putin: ready for war with Europe but does not want one
summary: On 29 October, after a call initiated by Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian PM Jonas Gahr Støre, Putin said Russia does not want war with Europe, that such a war would have no winners, and that Russia is ready if others prepare for one. Danish PM Mette Frederiksen was sceptical of the call. The FT reported Putin spent much of it on history; Støre disputes that.
corroboration: Kremlin remarks reported by TASS, the Telegraph, Kyiv Post and Bloomberg.
analysis: A familiar line, repeated from December 2025: reassurance paired with a warning. It does not change the evidence picture, which shows continuing hybrid pressure. The disagreement between the FT and Støre about what was said on the call is unresolved.

title: Telegraph: Moscow may demand NATO pullback to 1997 lines
summary: The Telegraph, citing unnamed diplomatic sources, reported that Russia is expected to seek a reduction of NATO's military presence in Eastern Europe to 1997 levels in peace talks, which could mean allied troops leaving Poland, the Baltic states and Finland. A European official said the position is the same as in January 2022. Russia has agreed to US-mediated talks with Ukraine in Abu Dhabi next month.
corroboration: One original report (Telegraph), widely repeated by Ukrainian and other outlets.
analysis: Not confirmed by any official. It is consistent with Russia's December 2021 demands, which makes it plausible, but it has not been formally announced. Note the tension with the Kremlin's 29 October statement ruling out European participation in the Abu Dhabi round, while the Telegraph says Moscow wants Europeans at the table.

title: Lithuania to introduce universal conscription in 2032
summary: After a State Defence Council meeting on 29 October, President Gitanas Nausėda said universal conscription will start in 2032, raising the annual intake from over 5,000 to about 7,500. The government wanted it sooner, but the military said it needs time to train instructors and build housing.
corroboration: LRT and BNS.
analysis: A long-term resilience measure, not a reaction to an imminent threat. The gap between the government's preferred pace and the army's readiness is worth noting.

title: Lithuania and Estonia say no US request to tone down warnings reached them
summary: Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said he had no information about a US request to soften statements on Russia and that Lithuania bases what it says on facts. Estonian PM Kristen Michal said no such complaints had reached him directly; the US message he heard at the NATO summit in Ankara was to spend more on defence. Outgoing foreign ministry secretary general Jonatan Vseviov said Estonia should never consider giving up its voice on Russia. Latvia has still not commented on the record; the three defence ministries did not answer Reuters.
corroboration: ERR (Estonian and Lithuanian statements) and LSM; the request itself still rests only on Reuters' four anonymous sources.
analysis: The denials cover official or direct requests, while Reuters described informal conversations with officials below the prime-minister level, so both versions can be true. Michal's comment also sits awkwardly with yesterday's reading of his earlier remarks that allies were asking Estonia to hold back. We have moved the claim to Contested.

title: Estonia and Latvia move to give border guards wider powers against Belarus-organised crossings
summary: At the Piusa border station on 30 October, Estonian Interior Minister Igor Taro said Baltic states could close their crossing points with Belarus for a while, as Poland did, and that Estonia is studying how far border guards may use force, up to lethal force. Latvian Interior Minister Jānis Dombrava said Latvia has amended its law so guards can use weapons against people who cross illegally or damage border infrastructure. Both said the Belarusian government organises the migration.
corroboration: ERR; LSM reported the Latvian legal change on 29 October.
analysis: A policy response to months of pressure, not to a new incident. The ministers expect crossings to ease in winter and rise again in spring. Closing crossings would hit cross-border trade and travel, so whether it happens is a political decision still to be made.

title: Russian national charged with spying after photographing Polish railways
summary: Police in Lower Silesia arrested a 55-year-old Russian national in Świdnica on 30 October while he was photographing trains and rail infrastructure with professional equipment. Investigators seized laptops, drives, phones and several identity documents and found hundreds of thousands of images of transport infrastructure, not only in Poland. He is charged with acting for a foreign intelligence service.
corroboration: Polish police via RMF24, relayed by Militarnyi, Meduza and others; one original source.
analysis: The service he allegedly worked for has not been named. Rail surveillance matters because Poland's railway was sabotaged in November 2025 and is a key route for aid to Ukraine. Not counted as a sabotage case, since the charge is espionage.

title: Russia: reports of men seized off the streets to sign army contracts
summary: Meduza, drawing on iStories, Verstka and rights groups, reports a new wave of complaints from relatives that men in Omsk and other cities are being detained and pressed to sign Defence Ministry contracts. Verstka counted complaints from 34 regions. The practice was first reported in Penza in June.
corroboration: Several Russian independent outlets, but most accounts are second-hand from relatives and activists; no official confirmation.
analysis: This fits the picture of a quiet, year-round recruitment drive for the Ukraine war rather than a mobilization aimed at NATO. It does not change the mobilization indicator, which stays at Watch.

title: Moscow keeps Europe out of peace talks while pressing demands on NATO
summary: ISW's 31 October assessment says the Kremlin has repeatedly demanded that European leaders stay out of the talks while renewing its call for NATO to return to its 1997 borders. Lavrov said Europeans are trying to squeeze into the process. Putin said after his call with Finland's and Norway's leaders that Russia wants full relations with Europe; a Finnish poll found three quarters of respondents backed President Stubb's decision to call.
corroboration: ISW; Yle; Kremlin statements reported by Russian state media.
analysis: The contradiction is in Moscow's own line: it wants Europe excluded from the talks but wants the talks to rewrite Europe's security arrangements. ISW's 1997 point cites its own earlier assessments rather than a new primary statement, so it does not yet confirm the Telegraph's report of a formal demand.

title: NATO mine-clearing ships visit Latvia
summary: Two ships of NATO's Standing Maritime Mine Countermeasures Group 1 arrived in Liepāja on 30 October.
corroboration: Latvian armed forces via LSM.
analysis: A routine visit by a standing NATO group. It is not a reaction to any new Russian move.

title: Unidentified object enters eastern Latvia from the Russia–Belarus border area
summary: On the evening of 1 November Latvia's armed forces warned of a threat in the airspace over the Krāslava and Ludza municipalities, near the borders with Belarus and Russia, and told residents to stay indoors. The alert lasted from about 18:59 to 19:30 local time; the military said the object left Latvian airspace across the Russian border. The Kyiv Independent reports that Latvia launched a BLAZE interceptor drone and that the object was likely a drone, but its origin is not yet clear.
corroboration: Latvian armed forces, relayed by Reuters, the Kyiv Independent and Izvestia; one original source.
analysis: The facts are thin. Earlier stray drones over Latvia have included Ukrainian drones pushed off course, reportedly by Russian jamming, and Russian ones, so neither origin should be assumed. Izvestia's headline calls it a drone and its related links point to Ukrainian drones, which goes further than the Latvian statement. A quick alert and interceptor launch show that Latvia's air-defence procedures are working.

title: NATO's top commander: Russia threatens NATO, but conflict is not inevitable
summary: In an interview with Latvian public media on 30 October, General Alexus Grynkewich, NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Europe, said Russia poses a threat to the alliance but he does not consider conflict inevitable, so NATO must make sure it is ready. He praised Latvia for reaching defence spending of 5% of GDP ahead of schedule and for its work on societal resilience.
corroboration: LSM interview, reported by Izvestia; consistent with his earlier public remarks in June and October.
analysis: Russian state media presented the interview as NATO preparing for conflict and placed it next to Putin's line that a war with Europe would have no winners. Grynkewich's actual message, readiness as a way to prevent war, matches the Lithuanian baseline: a low near-term threat and a longer-term risk that needs deterrence.

title: Estonia debates whether its warnings about Russia have become too predictable
summary: Former diplomat Jaap Ora, now a member of the opposition Isamaa party, told ERR that Estonia's Russia message has become predictable and risks partner fatigue, and that public statements should be measured. Prime Minister Kristen Michal said he will not hold back on Russia, and the outgoing foreign ministry secretary general said Estonia should never consider giving up its voice.
corroboration: ERR, 31 October and 1 November.
analysis: This is fallout from Reuters' anonymous-source report that the Pentagon asked the Baltic states to tone down their rhetoric. It is a domestic argument about style and influence, not new evidence about Russian intentions or about the request itself, which remains contested.

title: Satellite imagery shows a large Russian radar under construction in Kaliningrad
summary: Imagery analysed by the satellite company ICEYE and reported by FAZ and Stars and Stripes on 21 October shows a large over-the-horizon radar being built near Gvardeysk, about 37 km from the Polish border, with three antenna arrays each roughly 500 m long. ICEYE also counted more than 20 signals-intelligence and electronic-warfare sites across the exclave.
corroboration: ICEYE imagery via FAZ and Stars and Stripes; also discussed by the Robert Lansing Institute (commentary). No Russian or NATO official comment.
analysis: Added as a catch-up because earlier editions missed it. The construction is well documented, but claimed ranges of around 3,000 km are projections, and it is not known whether the radar works. It fits the baseline's judgement that Russia keeps building long-term military capacity, but a radar is a sensor, not a sign of imminent attack.

title: European intelligence officials say Russia targets defence-industry people and supply chains
summary: An Al Jazeera overview on 29 October brings together reports that representatives of five EU intelligence agencies told the Financial Times that Russia wants to kill European defence executives and disrupt their supply chains, and that FAZ reported incendiary devices planted in offices of two defence-technology firms in Munich. It also recalls the August plot against cargo planes at Leipzig/Halle, which the European Commission attributed to Russia.
corroboration: FT and FAZ reporting, summarised by Al Jazeera; the intelligence officials are not named.
analysis: The overview collects earlier reports rather than breaking new cases, so nothing here is counted as a new sabotage case. The pattern fits the baseline's warnings about preparation for disruptive operations, but the claim of plans to kill executives rests on unnamed officials.

title: Poland reinforces the Kaliningrad border after warnings of possible Russian sabotage
summary: Polish police launched a special operation along the border with Russia's Kaliningrad exclave, sending extra officers and counter-terrorism units to the Warmia-Masuria and Podlasie provinces and working with the army, Border Guard and security services. National police chief Marek Boroń said the measures follow information from security services about possible incidents that could lead to sabotage. An order puts officers on full readiness from 2 to 8 November; police had earlier denied it was linked to political tensions in Warsaw. The broadcaster RMF, citing unnamed sources, reports that Poland's Military Intelligence Service and allied agencies warned of possible sabotage and even incursions by armed groups.
corroboration: Police chief on the record via RMF and TVP World; Notes from Poland and UNITED24 relay RMF. The armed-groups detail rests on RMF's anonymous sources only.
analysis: The operation itself is confirmed; the threat behind it is described only in general terms. Authorities call it preventive and no incident has been reported. It fits the baseline's warnings about preparation for disruptive operations and Poland's experience of rail sabotage in 2025, but readers should not treat it as a sign that an attack from Kaliningrad is imminent.

title: Estonia deports a Russian citizen over contacts with Russian intelligence
summary: On 2 November Estonia's Police and Border Guard Board deported a Russian citizen and barred him from the Schengen area, on the recommendation of the Internal Security Service (KAPO). KAPO said he kept in contact with Russian intelligence officers and people working for them, travelled regularly to Russia and was in contact with sanctioned individuals. He worked for a Russia-linked policy centre that KAPO and media associate with Kremlin influence networks.
corroboration: KAPO statement via ERR, relayed by Militarnyi and European Pravda; one original source.
analysis: This is an administrative expulsion, not a conviction, and KAPO has not made its evidence public, so the man is not named here. It is consistent with the baseline's warnings about hostile intelligence services and influence operations in the region. No Russian reaction was found.

title: Latvia's 1 November air alert: interceptor self-destructed, object still unidentified
summary: New details from LSM, relayed by European Pravda: the orange alert over Krāslava and Ludza began at 18:59, the object left Latvian airspace toward Russia about 17 minutes later, and Latvia's BLAZE interceptor drone, used for the first time, was ordered to self-destruct at 19:19 so it would not cross the border. Defence Minister Raivis Melnis said the army keeps watching the airspace and is ready to respond again.
corroboration: Latvian armed forces and defence minister via LSM; relayed by European Pravda, Militarnyi and Izvestia.
analysis: There is still no official identification. Izvestia's headline calls it a drone and links to stories about Ukrainian drones falling in the Baltics, but its own text speaks only of an unidentified object. The interceptor did not reach the target, which shows the limits of new counter-drone tools against short incursions.

title: Catch-up: the 18 October drone in Lithuania came via Poland and carried explosives
summary: European Pravda, recapping recent incidents, reports that Lithuania says the drone whose debris was found on 18 October entered from Poland and carried explosives, and that Ukraine's foreign ministry spokesperson expressed regret, saying it was likely the result of Russian electronic warfare. Latvian forces also found wreckage of a crashed drone on 24 October.
corroboration: Lithuanian and Ukrainian official positions as reported by European Pravda; not checked here against Lithuanian primary sources.
analysis: Ukraine's expression of regret implies the drone was Ukrainian; the claim that Russian jamming pushed it off course is plausible, given documented interference, but unproven. It is a reminder that not every drone over the Baltics is a Russian provocation, and that Russian electronic warfare can still create risk for NATO territory.

title: Poland says it prevented a possible provocation on the Kaliningrad border
summary: Prime Minister Donald Tusk told a cabinet meeting on 3 November that border guards reported people with flashlights moving near the border with Russia's Kaliningrad region shortly after midnight, near Sępopol in Warmia-Masuria. Forces were moved in quickly, nobody crossed and the group withdrew into Kaliningrad. Tusk said Polish and allied services, and NATO's top commander Alexus Grynkewich, had warned of sabotage or more serious provocations in the first half of November, including a possible incursion by armed people; he added that he could not be certain a provocation was intended and expects Russian pressure to continue. Police chief Marek Boroń said the operation, including counter-terrorism units and GROM special forces, runs until at least 8 November.
corroboration: Tusk via RMF24, AP, Reuters-based reports, CBS, Meduza and LIGA; all relay the same statement, so this is one source on the incident itself.
analysis: The incident is minor and ambiguous: a sighting, not an attempted crossing. What gives it weight is the earlier warnings, now confirmed on the record by the prime minister, though their evidence is not public. Headlines about a 'thwarted provocation' run ahead of what Tusk himself claimed. It is consistent with the baseline's warnings about preparation for disruptive operations.

title: Latvia: one drone was most likely a Russian Geran, the other looked Ukrainian
summary: At a briefing on 3 November Latvia's armed forces said the drone that crossed into Krāslava and Ludza on 1 November was most likely a Russian Geran type; it is not known whether it was armed, and it flew back into Russia. A second drone triggered an alert in Balvi and Ludza from 00:10 to 00:35 on 3 November; NATO air-policing fighters and two Latvian interceptor drones were launched, and initial visual identification suggested a type used by Ukraine. It may have crashed in Balvi district, where National Guard units are searching.
corroboration: Latvian armed forces via LSM and Reuters; European Pravda reported the alerts. One original source.
analysis: The Russian attribution is notable because Russian state media had framed the 1 November alert around stray Ukrainian drones. Both identifications are provisional and based on tracking and visual observation, not wreckage. Whatever their origin, two incursions in three days near the Russia–Belarus border show the air-defence pressure on Latvia's east.

title: Lithuania: German brigade steps up surveillance of Kaliningrad and Belarus
summary: After Poland's reports, soldiers of the Bundeswehr's 45th Armoured Brigade in Lithuania began extra monitoring of threats from Belarus and Kaliningrad, using electronic intelligence equipment and drone-detection systems, according to LRT as relayed by UNN. Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said Lithuanian and Polish intelligence had exchanged information on possible threats and that protection of the Kaliningrad border had already been strengthened weeks earlier. Lithuanian authorities said no further reinforcement is needed for now; army support for border guards there was earlier extended to mid-November.
corroboration: LRT via UNN; earlier ELTA and LRT reports on the army deployment.
analysis: Lithuania's response is calm and measured, which fits the baseline view of a low conventional threat with hybrid risks. Not checked against LRT's original article.

title: Moscow calls the Polish sabotage warnings fake
summary: Russia's embassy in Warsaw, quoted by TASS, said Poland's information space is filled with militarist rhetoric, including fake news about possible sabotage. TASS noted that Tusk gave no evidence. No comment was found from the Kremlin, the foreign ministry or Kaliningrad's authorities. Separately, on 1 November Dmitry Medvedev mocked claims of a Russian hand in Poland's political crisis in a post ending with a phrase that can be read as menacing.
corroboration: TASS and Izvestia; Meduza, the Moscow Times and AP report no Russian response beyond this.
analysis: Both sides make claims without public evidence: Poland has not published its intelligence, and Russia offers only a blanket denial. Polish investigations have since contradicted Russian denials of earlier sabotage cases in Poland, which weakens this one.

title: Context: US-brokered talks set for Abu Dhabi as Washington urges restraint in rhetoric
summary: US envoy Steve Witkoff said trilateral talks with Ukraine and Russia would be held in Abu Dhabi on 10–11 November. Reuters reported last week that Pentagon officials privately asked Baltic allies to tone down public warnings about Russia, and that US force posture in Europe is under review. Tusk's public warnings this week show Poland is not following that advice.
corroboration: Reuters reporting relayed by FinChannel and the Moscow Times; no Baltic official commented on the record.
analysis: A ceasefire in Ukraine is the main development that could free Russian forces and shift the baseline's long-term risk closer; nothing so far suggests a deal is near. The gap between US calls for restraint and Polish and Baltic public warnings is a real policy difference, not a factual dispute.

title: Polish minister: a large provocation could be staged to blame Ukrainians
summary: Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister coordinating Poland's special services, said on TVN24 on 4 November that something 'very massive' could happen on both sides of the border, with the aim of pinning the blame on Ukrainians. He called the warnings serious and said they concern both Poland and the Baltic states, but described the information as imprecise and said he could not confirm that the plan involved crossing from Kaliningrad. Regional police in Olsztyn said preventive operations continue in border counties.
corroboration: Reported by infoSecurity24 from the TVN24 interview; consistent with Tusk's 3 November remarks and with the NATO commander's warning reported by Stars and Stripes. The intelligence itself is not public.
analysis: A false-flag framing is plausible given past Russian information operations, and the baseline warns of preparation for disruptive operations. But this is a warning about intent, not evidence of an operation, and the minister himself stressed its imprecision. It should be read as Poland trying to inoculate the public in advance.

title: Germany arrests suspected organiser of the Starlink arson near Warsaw
summary: Stuttgart prosecutors said on 3 November that special police arrested a Turkish citizen in the Reutlingen district who is suspected of ordering the 23 September fire at a Starlink ground station in Wola Krobowska, south of Warsaw, and of hiring two other Turkish men to carry it out. A court ordered him held on strong suspicion of preparing a terrorist offence. Two men aged 38 and 34 were detained in October on Polish warrants. Warsaw blames Russian intelligence; Der Spiegel reports the trail leads to a Turkish organised-crime group that may have worked for Russian services.
corroboration: Stuttgart prosecutors and the Baden-Württemberg police; Der Spiegel reporting relayed by Euromaidan Press. The Russian link rests on Polish official attribution and press reporting.
analysis: This is the most concrete development of the day: a real arrest, with courts involved in three countries. It fits the baseline pattern of Russian services using hired criminals and proxies. The suspects are presumed innocent, and the Russian link has not been proven in court.

title: US and German forces in Europe tighten force protection
summary: Stars and Stripes reports that NATO's top commander, General Alexus Grynkewich, was among those who warned Poland of possible provocations on its north-eastern border. US European Command launched a 'See Something, Do Something' campaign urging personnel to vary routes, disable fitness-app geotagging and limit posts about travel. A senior German commander said on 1 November that security at German bases has been increased, after the Bundeswehr raised its sabotage threat level in October.
corroboration: Stars and Stripes; earlier German reporting on the Bundeswehr threat level (Süddeutsche Zeitung via Kyiv Post).
analysis: Allied militaries are treating sabotage as a real and ongoing risk to their own people and bases, which is consistent with the hybrid part of the baseline. These are protective measures, not signs that allies expect a military attack.

title: Lukashenko calls NATO an aggressive bloc but says Minsk and Moscow will attack no one
summary: Speaking at the Minsk conference on Eurasian security on 3 November, attended by Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, Belarusian leader Alexander Lukashenko said NATO has become an aggressive bloc with offensive potential and that Western leaders, who he claims are preparing for war around 2030, do not grasp how large such a clash would be. He said Russia and Belarus have no intention of attacking anyone.
corroboration: Izvestia (Russian state media); the conference is an annual Minsk–Moscow forum.
analysis: Standard rhetoric for this forum: it mirrors the Western '2030' debate back as Western aggression. The promise not to attack anyone carries little weight, since the same was said before February 2022, and the baseline notes Belarus's territory is increasingly used for Russian military purposes.

title: Russian state media: Poland's border operation is a domestic distraction
summary: RT argued that Tusk launched the counter-terrorism deployment to distract from Poland's power struggle over the Constitutional Tribunal, called his warnings unproven and recalled earlier Russian nuclear warnings over Kaliningrad. It offered no evidence about what happened at the border.
corroboration: RT only; it echoes the Russian embassy's 'fake news' line reported yesterday.
analysis: The piece shifts attention to Polish domestic politics and ignores that the warnings came from several allied services, including NATO's commander. It is a narrative, not counter-evidence. That Poland has not published its intelligence is a fair point, but it does not make the warnings false.

title: Context: the days to watch, from 6 to 11 November
summary: Poland's operation runs until at least 8 November; Poland's Independence Day is 11 November, and a PISM analyst told Wirtualna Polska that Russia and Belarus could time sabotage or a blackout to coincide with it. US-brokered Russia–Ukraine talks are planned in Abu Dhabi on 10–11 November, and a Pentagon review of US troop options in Europe was due to reach the defence secretary by 6 November, according to an August Reuters report.
corroboration: Wirtualna Polska (analyst); Kremlin confirmation of the talks via US News/Reuters; Defense News (Reuters, August).
analysis: These dates matter for the baseline: a ceasefire could in time free Russian forces, and any reduction of US troops would weaken deterrence. Neither has happened. The analyst's warning about 11 November is a reasonable judgement, not intelligence.

title: Lithuania expels three Ukrainians over paid tasks for hostile intelligence services
summary: Lithuania's State Security Department told BNS on 5 November that three Ukrainian citizens had received paid tasks over Telegram and other messaging apps from hostile foreign intelligence services, such as filming particular sites and interviewing certain people. Their residence permits were revoked, they were declared a threat to national security and banned from returning for five years; the Migration Department confirmed they have left. Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas also commented. No criminal investigation was opened.
corroboration: LRT and BNS, quoting the VSD and the Migration Department. The VSD did not name the foreign services or say where the three went.
analysis: This is exactly the recruitment pattern the 2026 threat assessment describes: low-cost, online tasking of people who need money. Expelling rather than prosecuting is a preventive tool, so the evidence has not been tested in court. That the people are Ukrainian is also a reminder that hostile services recruit from any community, and it should not be read as a judgement on Ukrainians in Lithuania.

title: Poland detains six over supplying Russia's military and espionage
summary: Poland's Internal Security Agency (ABW) said it had detained five Polish citizens aged 25 to 52 and a 37-year-old Russian citizen after 21 searches between 21 October and 2 November in the Warmia-Masuria, Pomerania and Greater Poland regions. All are charged with taking part in an organised criminal group that allegedly sent Russia large quantities of military components used for ammunition and weapons; four are also suspected of espionage. A court ordered three months' custody. Minister Tomasz Siemoniak said nearly 100 people have been charged in espionage and sabotage cases since January 2024.
corroboration: LIGA.net, citing the ABW and the minister; court custody order confirms the case is active.
analysis: A significant case, but about sanctions evasion and spying rather than an attack. It fits the baseline picture of Russian services working across the region through local networks. The suspects are presumed innocent.

title: Shoigu accuses Poland and the Baltic states of training people to undermine Russia
summary: At a press event for Russia's National Unity Day, Security Council Secretary Sergei Shoigu said Poland, the Baltic states and other countries are training people to work against Russia from within, often through NGOs and non-profits, and that the Security Council is dealing with it. Asked about this on 5 November, Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said Russia's foreign-policy concept allows 'symmetrical and asymmetrical' responses to unfriendly actions.
corroboration: TASS (Zakharova); Interia via Bytes Europe (Shoigu). No supporting evidence was offered.
analysis: The accusation comes days after Poland and Lithuania went public about Russian sabotage and spying, and mirrors those charges back. It gives Moscow a ready narrative for restrictions at home and, potentially, a pretext for 'responses' abroad. It is not evidence of military planning, and Zakharova's formula is a standard phrase rather than a specific threat.

title: Romanian court orders arrest of alleged coordinator of 2024 energy-site sabotage plot
summary: The Bucharest Court of Appeals, at the request of anti-terrorism prosecutors (DIICOT), on 2 November ordered the arrest in absentia of a 35-year-old Cuban man living in Russia. Prosecutors say he paid a former Colombian soldier in mid-2024 to travel to Romania, scout oil wells and a gas station near Bucharest and prepare attacks; that man was stopped by police and the Romanian Intelligence Service, and was sentenced to six years in 2025.
corroboration: AGERPRES via CiberCuba; earlier Romanian conviction of the accomplice. The Russian link rests on the prosecutors' case.
analysis: Further evidence of the proxy model the baseline warns about: foreign nationals hired from a distance for sabotage. The suspect is in Russia, so the order is largely symbolic. Romania is outside the Baltic region, but the same networks have been linked to cases in Poland and Germany.

title: OSINT map shows GPS interference along almost the whole eastern flank
summary: Militarnyi reported on 4 November that an ItaMilRadar map, built from AirNav Radar flight data, showed GNSS interference on 3 November from the Baltic Sea to the Black Sea, with the most intense disruption near Kaliningrad, over Lithuania and eastern Poland, and around Romania and Bulgaria.
corroboration: One OSINT source relayed by Militarnyi; consistent with earlier government and maritime monitoring.
analysis: These maps show where aircraft report degraded navigation, not where jammers are; some interference comes from Russian air defence and from Ukraine-related electronic warfare. Even so, the pattern around Kaliningrad matches what Lithuania's assessment describes. Nothing in it suggests a new escalation.

title: Context: the days to watch, 6–11 November
summary: Poland's Kaliningrad border operation runs until at least 8 November and Poland marks Independence Day on 11 November. The Kremlin has confirmed that a Russian delegation led by Vladimir Medinsky will attend trilateral talks with the US and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi on 10–11 November. The Pentagon's review of US forces in Europe was due to deliver options to the defence secretary around 6 November; no decision has been announced. The Robert Lansing Institute speculates that Moscow hopes to deal with Washington directly over European security after the US midterm elections.
corroboration: APA (Kremlin confirmation); Breaking Defense commentary on the review; Lansing Institute (commentary, no named sources for its view of Kremlin intent).
analysis: A ceasefire could in time free Russian forces and a large US drawdown would weaken deterrence; either would move the picture away from the baseline. Neither has happened. The Lansing piece is commentary and is not used for any rating.
